title: The Man with the Unlucky Face (HI)
summary: Akbar sentences a merchant to death because seeing his face brought bad luck. Birbal shows the Emperor whose face was truly bringing misfortune.
full_text:
In the city of Agra lived a merchant named Ramu whose face was considered unlucky by superstitious neighbors. One morning, Emperor Akbar looked out of his bedroom window and his eyes fell upon Ramu walking along the riverbank.

That morning, Akbar stubbed his toe on a stone, received news that a royal supply ship had sunk in the Yamuna, and at lunch, a hot cup of soup spilled over his lap.

Furious and convinced that Ramu was a harbinger of doom, Akbar ordered the merchant arrested: 'His unlucky face has brought me three disasters before noon! Hang him at the city gates tomorrow morning so that no other citizen suffers his evil eye!'

Ramu wept in the dungeon. In despair, his wife appealed to Birbal.

The next morning, as Ramu stood upon the scaffold with the noose around his neck, Birbal arrived with Emperor Akbar.

Birbal stepped forward: 'Sire, before this man is hanged, he has one question for the Emperor.'

Akbar nodded: 'Let him speak.'

Birbal asked: 'Ramu, who was the very first person you saw yesterday morning when you stepped out of your house?'

Ramu replied: 'My lord, as I walked toward the river, I looked up at the palace balcony and saw the radiant face of our Emperor Akbar!'

Birbal turned to Akbar with profound solemnity:

'Consider this carefully, Your Majesty. Yesterday morning, you saw Ramu's face, and you merely stubbed your toe and spilled your soup.

'But Ramu looked upon Your Majesty's face, and as a direct result, he has lost his liberty, his family is weeping in terror, and he is now about to lose his life upon the gallows!

'Now tell me, Sire—before God and this assembly—whose face has proven to be the more unlucky of the two?'

Akbar stood frozen. The mirror of Birbal's logic held up his own superstition and cruelty for all to see. Ashamed of his irrational anger, Akbar ordered Ramu released immediately, granted him a purse of gold coins, and vowed never to let superstition guide imperial justice again.
